title: The Battle of Saraighat
body: In the 17th century, Aurangzeb sent Mughal forces into the Northeast and they briefly captured the Ahom capital, Garhgaon. The Mughals had more men and a larger fleet of river boats. The Ahoms, however, knew their land well: dense forests, hills and rivers. Using persistent guerrilla tactics, they pushed back the attack. In 1671, at the Battle of Saraighat on the Brahmaputra River near present-day Guwahati, the Ahom commander Lachit Borphukan and his 10,000 men defeated a Mughal force of 30,000 soldiers. The Mughal general Ram Singh later praised the Ahom warriors, saying that every Assamese soldier was expert in rowing boats, shooting arrows, digging trenches and wielding guns and cannons. The Ahoms were able to preserve their independence.

title: A merchant of Surat
body: Imagine a cloth merchant in the port of Surat in the 17th century. He has sold a large shipment of cotton textiles and must pay a supplier of dyes who lives in a distant inland town, across the borders of more than one kingdom. The roads are long, and armies and robbers sometimes plunder travellers. Instead of sending a servant with bags of silver coins, the merchant writes a hundi, a written instruction asking a trusted banker in the supplier's town to pay the amount. Trader communities such as the Marwaris had built such systems of credit and trust, which worked across different political regimes and without the participation of the ruling classes.
